lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What is the difference between [call|call|c], [apply|apply|c], and [bind|bind|c]?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: All three let you choose what {this} means inside a function. The difference is when the function runs, and how you pass the arguments.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: First, {this}. Inside a function, {this} is the object the function is working on.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Here is a function that reads [this.name|this dot name|c]. And two objects, john and jimmy.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: [call|Call|c] plugs an object into {this}, and runs the function right now. Arguments go in one by one.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: [apply|Apply|c] does the same. But the arguments come in as an array.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: A trick to remember: call is for commas, apply is for arrays.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: [bind|Bind|c] does not run anything. It returns a new function, with {this} fixed for good.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: You can preset arguments too. Here Hi is already filled in.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What if I call a bound function with a different {this}?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It is ignored. A bound function keeps its first {this}.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And bind returns a new function. The original stays untouched.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Why do people use bind in real code?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Because a method loses its {this} when you pass it around as a callback.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Take the method out of the object, call it, and this dot name is {undefined}.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Bind it to the object first, and it works again.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So call and apply run now. Bind gives you a function for later.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Got it. Call, apply, now. Bind, later.
